proposal.title: The Atlantic Catalogued 50 Norm-Bending Moments From Trump's First Two Years
proposal.description_short: The Atlantic's 2019 project selected 50 incidents from Trump's first two years and framed them as improbable, norm-bending and destructive.
proposal.description_medium: In January 2019, The Atlantic published an interactive catalog of 50 incidents from Donald Trump’s first two years as president. The magazine said its research team narrowed hundreds of candidates and ranked the selections subjectively for outlandishness and importance. The project documents the magazine’s framing of the presidency, not a specific institutional reform.
proposal.description_long: The Atlantic’s January 2019 “Unthinkable” project surveyed Donald Trump’s first two years in office through a ranked list of 50 incidents. The page says the editors began with hundreds of moments and selected incidents they considered improbable, norm-bending and destructive; it describes the ranking as subjective and based on both outlandishness and importance. Its entries include Trump praising a congressman who had body-slammed a reporter, a secretary of state’s ouster by tweet, and the first president to complain about an election he had won. In a contemporaneous WBUR interview, Atlantic editor Adrienne LaFrance explained that the series examined norm-breaking in communication and treatment of institutions, from small daily acts to larger ones. These sources support a description of an editorial survey and its stated lens. They do not identify a particular constitutional reform or establish the abstract claim that a continuing pattern was “treated as structural.” The replacement title and text therefore describe the project itself and attribute its interpretation to its publishers.

proposal.title: Brian Murphy’s Complaint Alleges DHS Officials Sought Changes to Threat Assessments
proposal.description_short: Brian Murphy’s 2020 whistleblower complaint alleged DHS leaders pressed for changes to threat assessments involving white supremacists and Antifa; the claims are allegations.
proposal.description_medium: Brian Murphy filed a whistleblower reprisal complaint with DHS’s inspector general on September 8, 2020. These are complaint allegations, not findings.
proposal.description_long: On September 8, 2020, Brian Murphy, then a senior official in the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Intelligence and Analysis, filed a whistleblower reprisal complaint with the DHS inspector general. The House Intelligence Committee released the complaint the next day. In it, Murphy alleged that in May and June 2020, acting deputy secretary Ken Cuccinelli asked him to change the Homeland Threat Assessment so that the white-supremacist threat appeared less severe and information about violent left-wing groups was included. Murphy also alleged that, during meetings from late May through July, Cuccinelli and acting secretary Chad Wolf directed him to modify intelligence assessments concerning Antifa and “anarchist” groups to align with President Trump’s public comments. The complaint records Murphy’s allegations and his account that he declined to make changes based on political rhetoric. It does not itself establish an inspector-general or congressional finding that the officials issued the instructions or that the assessments were changed. The original TrumpFile summary did not provide this primary document; the committee release and complaint support an attributed allegation rather than a proven cover-up.

The court action was a temporary restraint during litigation; the cited sources do not describe a government shutdown or an injunction against firing federal employees. The original title and short description refer to shutdown-related firings, while the linked reporting and court order concern the separate funding-freeze dispute. This revised account identifies the court, date, instrument, and scope, and avoids describing the TRO as a final merits judgment.

proposal.title: GAO and EPA OIG Flagged Pruitt-Era Booth Spending and Premium Travel
proposal.description_short: GAO found $43,238.68 spent on Scott Pruitt’s office booth without advance notice; EPA OIG estimated $123,942 in excessive premium airfare costs.
proposal.description_medium: The Government Accountability Office found that EPA obligated $43,238.68 for a soundproof privacy booth in Administrator Scott Pruitt’s office without required advance notice to congressional appropriations committees. EPA’s inspector general later estimated $123,942 in excessive first- and business-class airfare costs because the travel exception lacked sufficient justification and initially lacked proper approval. These reports establish oversight findings, not personal enrichment or criminal corruption.
proposal.description_long: Two oversight reviews substantiate specific spending findings involving EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt. In April 2018, the Government Accountability Office concluded that EPA violated the appropriations-notice requirement and the Antideficiency Act when it obligated $43,238.68 for a soundproof privacy booth in the administrator’s office without advance notice to congressional appropriations committees. EPA said the booth supported classified and private calls. In a separate May 2019 audit, EPA’s inspector general reviewed 40 trips and about $985,037 in associated costs for March through December 2017, including staff and protective-detail expenses. The audit estimated $123,942 in excess airfare for Pruitt and accompanying security agents’ first- or business-class travel because the exception initially lacked sufficient justification. It also noted that 16 trips included travel to or stops in Tulsa, where Pruitt had a personal residence. These reports document agency spending and control violations or questioned costs; they do not establish that Pruitt was criminally convicted of corruption or that each expense was personally improper. The grounded title keeps the booth and airfare findings distinct and attributes each to the responsible oversight body.

proposal.title: Trump Pardoned Steve Bannon Among 73 Pardons Granted on January 20, 2021
proposal.description_short: A January 20, 2021 clemency statement lists 73 pardons and 70 commutations, including a full pardon for Steve Bannon.
proposal.description_medium: The January 20, 2021 clemency statement says President Donald Trump pardoned 73 people and commuted the sentences of 70 others in his final hours in office. It specifically lists a full pardon for Steve Bannon, who faced federal charges related to the We Build the Wall fundraising effort. proposal.description_long: NBC News reported that in the final hours of his first presidency, Donald Trump granted clemency to 143 people: 73 received pardons and 70 had sentences commuted. Former White House adviser Steve Bannon was among those pardoned. The article says Bannon had been indicted with three others on conspiracy charges involving wire fraud and money laundering related to the “We Build the Wall” crowdfunding campaign. Prosecutors alleged that hundreds of thousands of dollars in donations were diverted for personal expenses; Bannon had not been tried on those charges when he received clemency, so the allegations were not resolved at trial. NBC separately notes that Trump had pardoned Michael Flynn and Roger Stone and commuted Paul Manafort’s sentence earlier, rather than including all three in this final-hours group. The reported 143 figure therefore covers different forms of clemency and does not support describing every recipient as an ally or every grant as a pardon. The revised title keeps Bannon’s pardon and the group total while distinguishing pardons from commutations, prior grants, and unresolved criminal allegations.
